summary: Describes an Application Level Gateway for SNMP that statically maps IP addresses inside SNMP packet payloads from one group to another, as used with address translation.

eli5.summary: When a network translator changes addresses, SNMP messages carry addresses inside. This fixes those inside addresses too.

questions: how does snmp work across nat
what is an snmp application level gateway
why do snmp messages contain ip addresses
how does snmpv3 break with nat
subtitle: Translating IP addresses inside SNMP messages when NAT changes them.

tldr.problem: When Network Address Translation is used to hide private IP addresses, management messages (SNMP) carry those internal addresses in their payloads. A management station looking at these addresses will see the hidden internal addresses, not the external ones, creating confusion and breaking discovery tools.
tldr.mechanism: An SNMP Application Level Gateway (ALG) intercepts SNMP messages, parses them for IP addresses in various formats, and rewrites them according to a translation table before forwarding, just as the NAT rewrites the IP packet headers.
tldr.outcome: A basic implementation can handle simple cases transparently. An advanced implementation can handle IP addresses embedded in table indices and other complex formats, but introduces complexity and potential packet size changes that can cause SNMPv3 and other issues.

today: RFC 2962 is an Informational RFC describing a technique that sees limited deployment. Most modern networks avoid the problem by deploying SNMPv3 with proper security policies and end-to-end management networks that bypass NAT. SNMP ALGs are most relevant in organizations that must manage multiple private networks with overlapping addresses and lack a dedicated management network. SNMP proxies remain preferable for secure, auditable management across trust boundaries.

sections.title: SNMP in Translated Networks
sections.content:
Network management typically relies on SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) to monitor and configure devices. When a network uses Network Address Translation to shield private addresses from the outside, a management station outside the NAT cannot directly monitor devices inside—or rather, it can, but it will see only the external address of the NAT gateway, not the individual devices behind it.

However, SNMP queries ask devices for information about their neighbors. A router inside the NAT might reply "my neighbor is 192.168.1.1," but a manager outside the NAT expects addresses in the externally visible realm. Without address translation in SNMP messages, the manager sees internal addresses that are meaningless to it, discovering and trying to manage equipment that it cannot actually reach. The SNMP Application Level Gateway (ALG) translates these addresses inside the message payload, maintaining a coherent view for the manager.
sections.eli5: A router behind NAT tells the manager "my neighbor is 192.168.1.1." But the manager is outside NAT and cannot reach that address. The SNMP ALG translates the address inside the message so the manager sees the correct external address.

sections.title: Where IP Addresses Hide in SNMP
sections.content:
SNMP messages are encoded using ASN.1 and the Basic Encoding Rules (BER). IP addresses appear in four contexts: as bare IpAddress base types in object values, embedded in object instance identifiers (which form the OID), encoded inside OCTET STRING values using textual conventions like TAddress or InetAddress, and embedded in the OIDs derived from such conventions.

A basic SNMP ALG handles only the first case: it looks for the IpAddress tag (0x40) and replaces the 4-byte address if it matches the translation table. This requires no MIB knowledge and does not change packet size. An advanced SNMP ALG scans for specific OIDs that are known to contain addresses, replacing addresses that appear as index values or in other formats. This requires building a MIB-aware OID translation table and is much more computationally expensive.
sections.eli5: IP addresses hide in four ways inside SNMP messages. The simple fix is to find and replace just one type. The complex fix handles all four, but it is slow and needs to know about MIBs.

sections.title: Basic and Advanced Implementations
sections.content:
A basic SNMP ALG parses each SNMP message looking for the IpAddress tag, extracts the 4-byte address, checks it against the translation table, and replaces it if needed. It adjusts the UDP checksum to match the new payload. Since it only touches addresses in the IpAddress base type, the message size never changes, and the algorithm is simple to implement.

An advanced SNMP ALG must also handle IP addresses that are part of an OID. When an address is embedded in an OID, replacing it may change the OID's length (because of how OIDs are encoded in BER). This changes the SNMP message size, which can cause SNMPv3 messages to exceed the maximum message size the receiver is willing to accept, causing the message to be dropped silently. The advanced ALG must also maintain an OID translation table, requiring a MIB compiler to pre-populate it with all MIBs in use within the addressed realms.
sections.eli5: The simple version finds bare IP addresses and fixes them. The complex version also fixes addresses that are part of addresses lists, but this can change message size and break SNMPv3.

sections.title: Security Trade-offs
sections.content:
SNMPv1 and SNMPv2c offer weak security based on community strings sent in cleartext. An SNMP ALG does not need the community string to translate addresses, so it introduces no additional security problems in these versions.

SNMPv3, however, uses cryptographic authentication and encryption. The SNMPv3 message is authenticated as a whole, and the payload is encrypted. If an SNMP ALG modifies the message after the manager has signed it, the authentication fails. The ALG must therefore have access to all the localized keys and must track key changes. This creates a significant operational burden and a new security perimeter that must be protected. The RFC warns that deploying an SNMP ALG in an SNMPv3 environment requires great care and coordination.
sections.eli5: SNMPv1 and SNMPv2c have no encryption, so changing addresses is safe. SNMPv3 uses signatures, and changing anything breaks the signature. The ALG has to know all the secret keys.

sections.title: When ALGs Fail
sections.content:
Even an advanced SNMP ALG cannot claim full transparency. It can only translate data types it understands. If a MIB defines an IP address using a textual convention the ALG does not recognize, or if an application constructs IP address values in an unexpected way, the ALG will miss them. Management applications that rely on the lexicographic ordering of instance identifiers (the order in which OIDs are returned) may break when an advanced ALG changes that ordering by modifying address values embedded in OIDs.

Furthermore, SNMP ALGs only handle SNMP traffic. Operators often use other protocols—telnet, SSH—to configure and troubleshoot devices. These protocols are unaffected by SNMP ALG, so an operator is never truly hidden from the existence of NAT. An alternative approach is to use an SNMP proxy forwarder, which has the advantage of allowing different security policies inside and outside the boundary, but requires that the management application be aware of the proxy and that the application be configured to use it.
sections.eli5: An ALG cannot handle every possible way to encode an address, and some management tools will break. Also, it only fixes SNMP, not telnet or other protocols that operators use.
